## What happens to my Google / Gmail when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/google-gmail/

Google never hands over passwords. If you set up Inactive Account Manager, up to 10 people you chose can download the data you picked once your account goes inactive. Without it, immediate family or a representative can ask Google to close the account, release funds or provide some data, decided case by case.

Key facts:
- Passwords: never shared
- Plan ahead: Inactive Account Manager, up to 10 contacts
- No plan: deceased-user request (close, funds or data)
- Inactivity: personal accounts can be deleted after 2 years
- Inactive Account Manager waits between 3 and 18 months of inactivity (Google)
- The 2-year inactive-account policy applies regardless of your Inactive Account Manager settings

Documents heirs need:
- Your ID and the deceased person's Gmail address
- A death certificate
- For data requests, Google may ask for further legal documents such as a court order

What can't be recovered:
- Passwords and login access
- Account contents after a closure request: Google says it can't process a later request for the contents once you choose to close the account
- Everything, if the account is deleted under the 2-year inactivity policy

Timeline: Inactive Account Manager runs only after the inactivity period you set. Deceased-user requests are reviewed individually and Google gives no fixed timeframe.

Sources: https://support.google.com/accounts/troubleshooter/6357590, https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3036546, https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/12418290, https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/workspace/storage-policy-update/

Q: What happens to my Google / Gmail when I die?
A: Google never hands over passwords. If you set up Inactive Account Manager, up to 10 people you chose can download the data you picked once your account goes inactive. Without it, immediate family or a representative can ask Google to close the account, release funds or provide some data, decided case by case.

Q: Can my family log into my Gmail after I die?
A: Not with Google's blessing. Google doesn't share passwords. Use Inactive Account Manager so contacts can download data instead.

Q: Does Google delete inactive accounts?
A: Google's policy lets it delete personal accounts that have been inactive for 2 years.

Q: How long does Inactive Account Manager wait?
A: You choose the period. Google says it can act after 3 to 18 months of inactivity. Google's separate 2-year inactivity policy still applies.

Q: Should I request data or closure first?
A: Data first. Google says that if you close the account it can't later turn over its contents.

Q: Does Inactive Account Manager include YouTube?
A: Yes. Google's own example lists Blogger, Drive, Mail and YouTube among the data a contact can be given.


## What happens to my Google Photos when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/google-photos/

Google Photos lives inside your Google Account, so it follows Google's rules. Add Photos to Inactive Account Manager and your chosen contacts can download it after the inactivity period. Without a plan, family must use Google's deceased-user data request, which isn't guaranteed. Shared albums and Takeout backups made now are the safest route.

Key facts:
- Covered by Inactive Account Manager
- No plan: deceased-user data request, reviewed case by case
- Inactive accounts can be deleted after 2 years
- Back up now with Google Takeout

Documents heirs need:
- Death certificate
- Your ID and the account address
- Possibly further legal documents for a data request

What can't be recovered:
- Photos only stored in an account deleted for inactivity
- Contents of an account already closed at family's request

Timeline: Contacts get a download link only after the inactivity period you chose. Data requests have no published timeframe.

Sources: https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3036546, https://support.google.com/accounts/troubleshooter/6357590, https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/12418290

Q: What happens to my Google Photos when I die?
A: Google Photos lives inside your Google Account, so it follows Google's rules. Add Photos to Inactive Account Manager and your chosen contacts can download it after the inactivity period. Without a plan, family must use Google's deceased-user data request, which isn't guaranteed. Shared albums and Takeout backups made now are the safest route.

Q: Will my Google Photos be deleted when I die?
A: They can be deleted if the account stays inactive for 2 years, so set up Inactive Account Manager and a Takeout backup.

Q: Can I give someone my photos automatically?
A: Yes. Inactive Account Manager can share your Google Photos data with up to 10 contacts.

Q: How do I back up my Google Photos?
A: Use Google Takeout and select Google Photos; store the archive offline and in a second location.

Q: Can family request photos without a plan?
A: They can ask through Google's deceased-user form, but Google decides each request after review.


## What happens to my Apple iCloud when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/apple-icloud/

With a Legacy Contact, that person uses their access key and your death certificate to request your iCloud data, such as photos, messages, notes, files and backups. Without one, Apple requires legal documentation, often a court order; Apple says Australia and some other countries accept alternative documents. Keychain passwords and purchased media are never included.

Key facts:
- Legacy Contact needs: access key + death certificate
- Excluded: iCloud Keychain and purchased media
- No Legacy Contact: court order or local equivalent
- Australia: Apple accepts alternative documentation
- Access lasts 3 years from the first approved request, then the legacy account is permanently deleted
- On approval, the original Apple Account stops working and Activation Lock is removed from its devices

Documents heirs need:
- Legacy Contact route: the access key and a death certificate
- Without a Legacy Contact: death certificate plus a court order or the documentation Apple accepts in your country
- To delete the account: your own Apple Account and the required legal documents

What can't be recovered:
- iCloud Keychain passwords, passkeys and payment info
- Purchased movies, music, books and subscriptions
- Some end-to-end encrypted data may need a device passcode
- A passcode-locked device can't be unlocked by Apple without erasing it

Timeline: Apple reviews and verifies documentation before acting and doesn't publish a fixed processing time.

Sources: https://support.apple.com/en-us/102631, https://support.apple.com/en-us/102431

Q: What happens to my Apple iCloud when I die?
A: With a Legacy Contact, that person uses their access key and your death certificate to request your iCloud data, such as photos, messages, notes, files and backups. Without one, Apple requires legal documentation, often a court order; Apple says Australia and some other countries accept alternative documents. Keychain passwords and purchased media are never included.

Q: Does a Legacy Contact get my passwords?
A: No. Keychain passwords are excluded, so pair it with a password manager that has emergency access.

Q: What if no Legacy Contact was set?
A: Apple generally requires a court order for family to get the data.

Q: How long does a Legacy Contact have access?
A: Three years from when the first legacy account request is approved. After that, Apple permanently deletes the legacy account, so download anything you want to keep.

Q: Does Legacy Contact remove Activation Lock?
A: Yes. Apple says Activation Lock is removed from devices that use the original Apple Account once access is approved. The devices then need to be erased and restored before reuse.

Q: Can Apple unlock a dead person's iPhone?
A: No. Apple says it can't remove a device passcode without erasing the device. It may help remove Activation Lock so the device can be reused.


## What happens to my Facebook when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/facebook/

Facebook either memorialises your profile, adding 'Remembering' next to your name, or permanently deletes it, depending on what you chose in advance. A legacy contact you name can manage parts of a memorialised profile, such as a pinned tribute post, but can't log in or read your messages. Family can request memorialisation with proof of death.

Key facts:
- Options: memorialise or delete
- Legacy contact: can't log in or read messages
- You must be 18+ to choose a legacy contact
- Set in Accounts Centre → Memorialisation

Documents heirs need:
- Memorialisation: proof of death such as an obituary
- Removal: proof you're immediate family or the executor, such as a death certificate

What can't be recovered:
- Private messages
- Login access for anyone, including the legacy contact

Timeline: Requests are reviewed by Facebook; no fixed timeframe is published.

Sources: https://www.facebook.com/help/1568013990080948, https://www.meta.com/help/accounts-center/841741830388205/

Q: What happens to my Facebook when I die?
A: Facebook either memorialises your profile, adding 'Remembering' next to your name, or permanently deletes it, depending on what you chose in advance. A legacy contact you name can manage parts of a memorialised profile, such as a pinned tribute post, but can't log in or read your messages. Family can request memorialisation with proof of death.

Q: Can a legacy contact read my messages?
A: No. They can manage a pinned tribute post, profile photo and friend requests, but not messages. You can optionally let them download a copy of what you shared.

Q: Can family delete a Facebook account?
A: Verified immediate family or an executor can request removal.

Q: Can I choose deletion instead?
A: Yes. In the Memorialisation settings you can choose to have your account permanently deleted after your death.

Q: Is Instagram the same?
A: No. Instagram offers memorialisation and removal requests but works differently. See our Instagram page.


## What happens to my Instagram when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/instagram/

Instagram memorialises an account when it receives proof of death, such as an obituary. Nobody can log into a memorialised account, and its posts stay visible to the same audience. Verified immediate family can instead ask for the account to be removed, using documents such as a death certificate. Instagram doesn't give out passwords.

Key facts:
- Memorialise: anyone, with proof of death
- Remove: verified immediate family
- No login access for anyone
- Back up your own photos via Download your information

Documents heirs need:
- Memorialisation: proof of death, such as an obituary link
- Removal: documents such as the death certificate and proof you're immediate family or the estate representative

What can't be recovered:
- Direct messages
- Login access

Timeline: Instagram reviews each request; no fixed timeframe is published.

Sources: https://help.instagram.com/264154560391256

Q: What happens to my Instagram when I die?
A: Instagram memorialises an account when it receives proof of death, such as an obituary. Nobody can log into a memorialised account, and its posts stay visible to the same audience. Verified immediate family can instead ask for the account to be removed, using documents such as a death certificate. Instagram doesn't give out passwords.

Q: Can family get into an Instagram account?
A: No. Instagram doesn't give out login access to memorialised accounts.

Q: Does Instagram have a legacy contact?
A: Instagram supports memorialisation and removal requests. Check the current Accounts Centre settings for options.

Q: How do I save my Instagram photos?
A: Use Accounts Centre → Your information and permissions → Download your information.

Q: Can anyone request memorialisation?
A: Yes, with proof of death. Removal is limited to verified immediate family.


## What happens to my X (Twitter) when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/x-twitter/

X doesn't memorialise accounts and won't give anyone access, including family. An immediate family member or a person authorised to act for the estate can ask X to deactivate the account. X then asks for details of the deceased, a copy of the requester's ID and a death certificate. Download your own archive now if you want posts kept.

Key facts:
- No memorialisation
- No account access for family
- Deactivation on request
- Needs: requester ID + death certificate

Documents heirs need:
- Details of the deceased and their @username
- A copy of your government ID
- A copy of the death certificate

What can't be recovered:
- Direct messages
- Posts, once the account is deactivated, unless someone downloaded an archive beforehand

Timeline: X emails instructions after the request is submitted; no fixed processing time is published.

Sources: https://help.x.com/en/rules-and-policies/contact-x-about-a-deceased-family-members-account

Q: What happens to my X (Twitter) when I die?
A: X doesn't memorialise accounts and won't give anyone access, including family. An immediate family member or a person authorised to act for the estate can ask X to deactivate the account. X then asks for details of the deceased, a copy of the requester's ID and a death certificate. Download your own archive now if you want posts kept.

Q: Will X give my family my DMs?
A: No. X won't provide account access to anyone, including family.

Q: Can I keep a copy of my posts for family?
A: Yes. Request your archive in Settings → Your account → Download an archive of your data, and store it with your digital estate plan.

Q: Who can ask X to deactivate an account?
A: An immediate family member or someone authorised to act on behalf of the estate.


## What happens to my Microsoft / Outlook when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/microsoft-outlook/

Microsoft won't release a deceased person's Outlook.com or OneDrive content without a valid subpoena or court order, and even then it isn't guaranteed. You don't need to report the death. If nobody signs in, Outlook.com and OneDrive are frozen after 1 year, with content deleted soon after, and the Microsoft account expires after 2 years.

Key facts:
- Content release: subpoena or court order only
- Outlook.com/OneDrive frozen after 1 year inactive
- Account expires after 2 years inactive
- Closed accounts can be reopened within 60 days

Documents heirs need:
- If you have the password: nothing; you can close the account yourself
- Without access: a valid subpoena or court order served on Microsoft's registered agent (Microsoft won't act on faxed or emailed requests)

What can't be recovered:
- Email and OneDrive files, after the 1-year freeze and deletion
- All account data 60 days after closure

Timeline: 1 year of inactivity: Outlook.com and OneDrive frozen and content deleted shortly after. 2 years: the Microsoft account expires. After a closure, 60 days to change your mind before permanent deletion.

Sources: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/accounts-billing/manage/accessing-outlook-com-onedrive-and-other-microsoft-services-when-someone-has-died

Q: What happens to my Microsoft / Outlook when I die?
A: Microsoft won't release a deceased person's Outlook.com or OneDrive content without a valid subpoena or court order, and even then it isn't guaranteed. You don't need to report the death. If nobody signs in, Outlook.com and OneDrive are frozen after 1 year, with content deleted soon after, and the Microsoft account expires after 2 years.

Q: Can I get into my late parent's Outlook account?
A: Usually only with a court order, unless a legacy feature or password was planned in advance.

Q: Does Microsoft have a legacy contact feature?
A: Microsoft's official page on deceased users doesn't describe one. It points family to closing the account (if they have the password) or a court order. Plan with a password manager instead.

Q: How do I stop a dead person's Microsoft subscriptions?
A: Microsoft suggests cancelling via the bank: close the card or account, or revoke the payment authorisation.


## What happens to my LinkedIn when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/linkedin/

LinkedIn offers two options: close the account or memorialise the profile. Anyone connected or related by last name can report a member as deceased, and LinkedIn will memorialise the profile. Closing the account requires someone with legal authority to act for the estate, a death certificate and probate-type documents. LinkedIn never gives out passwords.

Key facts:
- Memorialise: report as deceased (connection or same surname)
- Close: needs legal authority
- Memorialised accounts are locked
- Data deleted within 30 days of closure

Documents heirs need:
- Member's full name, profile URL and your relationship
- Helpful: their email, date of death and an obituary link
- To close: death certificate plus Letters of Administration, Letters Testamentary, Letters of Representation or another court order

What can't be recovered:
- Login access and messages
- All profile data after closure

Timeline: After closure, LinkedIn says it can take up to 30 days to fully delete the data.

Sources: https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1336663, https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1380121

Q: What happens to my LinkedIn when I die?
A: LinkedIn offers two options: close the account or memorialise the profile. Anyone connected or related by last name can report a member as deceased, and LinkedIn will memorialise the profile. Closing the account requires someone with legal authority to act for the estate, a death certificate and probate-type documents. LinkedIn never gives out passwords.

Q: Will LinkedIn delete a dead person's profile?
A: Yes, on request. LinkedIn can memorialise or close it.

Q: Can family get a LinkedIn password?
A: No. LinkedIn says it won't disclose usernames or passwords to anyone, including family, under any circumstances.

Q: What's the difference between memorialising and closing?
A: Memorialising keeps the profile visible but locked; closing deletes it. Closing requires legal authority.


## What happens to my Crypto exchanges (Coinbase) when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/coinbase/

Crypto held on Coinbase forms part of your estate. Coinbase doesn't support beneficiary designations for individual accounts, so heirs need to know the account exists. The executor files an Executor Services claim with a death certificate, proof of authority such as probate or letters of administration, photo ID, and a signed letter naming the Coinbase account to receive the assets.

Key facts:
- No beneficiary designation
- Claim via Coinbase Executor Services
- Needs probate or equivalent authority
- Recipient may need a Coinbase account

Documents heirs need:
- Official death certificate
- Probate, Letters Testamentary, Letters of Administration, or a small estate affidavit where accepted
- Current government photo ID of the person named in those documents
- A signed letter directing transfer to a named Coinbase account and email

What can't be recovered:
- Funds in self-custody wallets if nobody has the seed phrase. No company can recover those.

Timeline: Coinbase reviews claims after receiving the documents; no fixed timeframe is published.

Sources: https://help.coinbase.com/en/coinbase/managing-my-account/other/how-do-i-gain-access-to-a-deceased-family-members-coinbase-account

Q: What happens to my Crypto exchanges (Coinbase) when I die?
A: Crypto held on Coinbase forms part of your estate. Coinbase doesn't support beneficiary designations for individual accounts, so heirs need to know the account exists. The executor files an Executor Services claim with a death certificate, proof of authority such as probate or letters of administration, photo ID, and a signed letter naming the Coinbase account to receive the assets.

Q: Can I name a beneficiary on Coinbase?
A: No. The assets pass according to your will or the law.

Q: What about crypto in a hardware wallet?
A: No company can recover it. Your heirs need the seed phrase or an inheritance setup.

Q: Do heirs need a Coinbase account?
A: Usually. The assets are transferred to a Coinbase account named in the executor's letter.

Q: Can I name a beneficiary on Coinbase?
A: No. Coinbase says beneficiary designations aren't supported for individual accounts.


## What happens to my Dropbox when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/dropbox/

Dropbox may give access to a deceased person's files, but only after reviewing proof of death and a valid court order showing you have a legal right to them. Access isn't guaranteed and can take time. Dropbox's own first suggestion is to check the person's computer, where the Dropbox folder often holds a synced copy of every file.

Key facts:
- Check the synced folder on their computer first
- Needs proof of death + court order
- Access not guaranteed
- Request via a Dropbox support ticket

Documents heirs need:
- Full name and Dropbox email of the deceased
- Your name, mailing address, email and relationship
- A photocopy of your government ID
- A valid court order establishing your right to the files

What can't be recovered:
- Files that only exist online, if the request is refused

Timeline: Dropbox says these requests 'can take some time' and gives no fixed timeframe.

Sources: https://help.dropbox.com/account-settings/access-account-of-someone-who-passed-away

Q: What happens to my Dropbox when I die?
A: Dropbox may give access to a deceased person's files, but only after reviewing proof of death and a valid court order showing you have a legal right to them. Access isn't guaranteed and can take time. Dropbox's own first suggestion is to check the person's computer, where the Dropbox folder often holds a synced copy of every file.

Q: Does Dropbox have a legacy contact?
A: No. Dropbox handles access requests through its support process.

Q: Is there a faster way into Dropbox files?
A: Yes. Look in the Dropbox folder on the person's computer, which often contains synced copies of everything.

Q: Does Dropbox have a legacy contact?
A: No. Requests go through a support ticket with legal documents.


## What happens to my WhatsApp when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/whatsapp/

WhatsApp doesn't memorialise accounts or offer a legacy contact. Accounts are generally deleted after 365 days without connecting to WhatsApp. Chats and media saved on the person's phone stay there until the app is removed, so the phone itself is usually the only way family can keep messages. Recipients keep their own copies of messages.

Key facts:
- No memorialisation or legacy contact
- Inactive accounts deleted after 365 days
- Local chats stay on the device until WhatsApp is removed
- Deletion can't be undone or restored

Documents heirs need:
- To keep chats: access to the unlocked phone (the passcode)

What can't be recovered:
- Chats, media and backups from a deleted account: WhatsApp says it can't restore or transfer them
- Contacts saved to the WhatsApp account are deleted with it

Timeline: Generally 365 days of inactivity before automatic deletion. A deliberate account deletion can take up to 90 days to complete.

Sources: https://faq.whatsapp.com/828406668498455, https://faq.whatsapp.com/2138577903196467

Q: What happens to my WhatsApp when I die?
A: WhatsApp doesn't memorialise accounts or offer a legacy contact. Accounts are generally deleted after 365 days without connecting to WhatsApp. Chats and media saved on the person's phone stay there until the app is removed, so the phone itself is usually the only way family can keep messages. Recipients keep their own copies of messages.

Q: Can family read a dead person's WhatsApp messages?
A: Only from the person's own unlocked phone or a backup they can open. WhatsApp doesn't provide access.

Q: Does a WhatsApp account delete itself?
A: Generally yes, after 365 days of inactivity.

Q: Do other people keep my messages?
A: Yes. Deleting an account doesn't remove other users' copies of messages you sent them.


## What happens to my YouTube when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/youtube/

YouTube channels belong to a Google Account, so Google's rules apply. With Inactive Account Manager you can share YouTube data with up to 10 trusted contacts after a period of inactivity, or have the account deleted. Without a plan, family use Google's deceased-user request. Google never shares passwords, and inactive accounts can be deleted after 2 years.

Key facts:
- Governed by your Google Account
- Inactive Account Manager can share YouTube data
- No passwords shared
- 2-year inactivity deletion can apply

Documents heirs need:
- Death certificate and the requester's ID for Google's deceased-user request
- Possibly further legal documents for data

What can't be recovered:
- Login access to the channel
- Everything, if the account is deleted for inactivity or closed before data is requested

Timeline: Shared data is released only after your chosen inactivity period. Deceased-user requests have no published timeframe.

Sources: https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3036546, https://support.google.com/accounts/troubleshooter/6357590, https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/12418290, https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9481328

Q: What happens to my YouTube when I die?
A: YouTube channels belong to a Google Account, so Google's rules apply. With Inactive Account Manager you can share YouTube data with up to 10 trusted contacts after a period of inactivity, or have the account deleted. Without a plan, family use Google's deceased-user request. Google never shares passwords, and inactive accounts can be deleted after 2 years.

Q: Will my YouTube channel stay up after I die?
A: It stays until the account is closed or deleted. Under Google's policy, personal accounts inactive for 2 years can be deleted.

Q: Can someone take over my YouTube channel?
A: Google won't hand over a login. Add trusted people through channel permissions while you're alive.

Q: Can I give someone my videos automatically?
A: Yes. Include YouTube in Inactive Account Manager.


## What happens to my Amazon & Kindle library when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/amazon-kindle/

Amazon only shares account details or takes most actions for the authorised estate representative. If the account is closed, all purchased digital content goes with it, including Kindle books and notes, Audible, Prime Video and Amazon Music purchases, and Amazon Photos. Download photos and invoices before any closure request is made.

Key facts:
- Only the estate representative can act fully
- Closure removes Kindle, Audible, Prime Video and Music purchases
- Gift card balances are lost on closure
- Contact: bereavement-support-cs@amazon.com

Documents heirs need:
- Death certificate
- Proof you're the estate's legal representative (such as probate or executor documents)
- Valid photo ID
- The account's email or phone number, or an order number to locate it

What can't be recovered:
- Kindle books, notes and highlights, Audible and other digital purchases, once the account is closed
- Amazon Photos content not downloaded beforehand
- Gift card balances
- Order history and invoices

Timeline: Amazon verifies the documents, then acts; no fixed timeframe is published. Documents are deleted after validation.

Sources: https://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html?nodeId=TzcJJiVFnIi3pG2yDA, https://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html?nodeId=GBDB29JHRPFBDVYV

Q: What happens to my Amazon & Kindle library when I die?
A: Amazon only shares account details or takes most actions for the authorised estate representative. If the account is closed, all purchased digital content goes with it, including Kindle books and notes, Audible, Prime Video and Amazon Music purchases, and Amazon Photos. Download photos and invoices before any closure request is made.

Q: Can I inherit someone's Kindle books?
A: Amazon's help pages describe no way to transfer purchased digital content, and closing the account removes it. Keep the account and its devices in mind before requesting closure.

Q: What can family do without probate?
A: With a death certificate, Amazon can terminate subscriptions, stop recurring deliveries and deactivate the account.

Q: Does closing Amazon close Audible too?
A: Yes. Amazon lists Audible, Prime Video, Amazon Music, Amazon Photos and Kindle among the services lost on closure.


## What happens to my PayPal when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/paypal/

PayPal only takes instructions from the authorised executor or administrator of the estate. In Australia, the executor emails PayPal a cover sheet, the account email, a death certificate, a grant of probate or letters of administration, and photo ID. Any remaining balance can be paid to the linked bank account or by wire transfer.

Key facts:
- Executor or administrator only
- AU: grant of probate or letters of administration
- Balance paid to linked bank or by wire
- AU email: bereavement@paypal.com.au

Documents heirs need:
- Cover sheet stating the holder has died and the executor wants the account closed
- The account's email address
- Death certificate
- Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration (or a statutory certificate if a statutory body is executor)
- Executor's government photo ID

What can't be recovered:
- Login access: PayPal closes or locks the account rather than transferring it

Timeline: PayPal reviews documents after receiving them; no fixed timeframe is published.

Sources: https://www.paypal.com/au/cshelp/article/how-do-i-close-the-paypal-account-of-a-deceased-relative-help220, https://www.paypal.com/us/cshelp/article/how-do-i-close-the-paypal-account-of-a-deceased-relative-help220

Q: What happens to my PayPal when I die?
A: PayPal only takes instructions from the authorised executor or administrator of the estate. In Australia, the executor emails PayPal a cover sheet, the account email, a death certificate, a grant of probate or letters of administration, and photo ID. Any remaining balance can be paid to the linked bank account or by wire transfer.

Q: Can family close a PayPal account?
A: Only via the executor or administrator. PayPal asks others to contact the executor.

Q: What happens to the money in PayPal?
A: PayPal can pay it to the bank account linked to the PayPal account or by wire transfer.

Q: Is the process the same in the US and UK?
A: No. Each PayPal country site lists different documents and contact addresses.


## What happens to my Steam when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/steam/

Steam games are licences, not property you own. The Steam Subscriber Agreement says your account is strictly personal and that accounts and subscriptions can't be transferred unless Valve specifically permits it. Valve also says it doesn't recognise transfers made outside Steam, including by operation of law. Don't count on passing a Steam library to heirs.

Key facts:
- Games are licences
- Account is 'strictly personal'
- No transfer unless Valve permits it
- Transfers by operation of law aren't recognised

Documents heirs need:
- Valve publishes no deceased-user process. Contact Steam Support for the account.

What can't be recovered:
- The game library itself, in most cases
- Steam Wallet funds and items tied to the account

Timeline: No published process or timeframe.

Sources: https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/english/

Q: What happens to my Steam when I die?
A: Steam games are licences, not property you own. The Steam Subscriber Agreement says your account is strictly personal and that accounts and subscriptions can't be transferred unless Valve specifically permits it. Valve also says it doesn't recognise transfers made outside Steam, including by operation of law. Don't count on passing a Steam library to heirs.

Q: Can I leave my Steam games in my will?
A: Valve's Subscriber Agreement says accounts and subscriptions can't be transferred unless Valve specifically permits it, so a will alone doesn't move them.

Q: Can my kids keep playing on my account?
A: The agreement says you may not share your password or account except as Valve authorises.

Q: Is this different from physical games?
A: Yes. Discs and cartridges are property; Steam purchases are licences.


## What happens to my game libraries (Steam, GOG, Epic, PlayStation, Xbox) when I die?
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/platforms/game-libraries/

In most cases your digital games can't be passed on. Steam, Epic, PlayStation and Xbox license games to you personally and say the licence isn't transferable. Family can usually only stop charges or close the account. Write down what you own, and keep saves or mods backed up separately.

Key facts:
- Steam: licences, not transferable (Subscriber Agreement)
- Epic: personal, non-transferable licence; account can't be given away
- PlayStation (AU): licence not transferable unless local law requires
- Xbox: personal, non-transferable licence to currency and virtual goods
- GOG: no official bereavement policy we could verify

What can't be recovered:
- Purchased game libraries (licences end with the account)
- Wallet balances and in-game currency
- Cloud saves if the account is closed

Sources: https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/, https://legal.epicgames.com/epicgames/tos, https://www.playstation.com/en-au/legal/psn-terms-of-service/, https://www.microsoft.com/en-au/servicesagreement, https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/account-billing/accessing-outlook-com-onedrive-and-other-microsoft-services-when-someone-has-died-ebbd2860-917e-4b39-9913-212362da6b2f

Q: What happens to my game libraries (Steam, GOG, Epic, PlayStation, Xbox) when I die?
A: In most cases your digital games can't be passed on. Steam, Epic, PlayStation and Xbox license games to you personally and say the licence isn't transferable. Family can usually only stop charges or close the account. Write down what you own, and keep saves or mods backed up separately.

Q: Can I leave my Steam library to someone?
A: Steam's Subscriber Agreement says subscriptions are licences, Valve doesn't recognise transfers outside Steam (including by operation of law), and subscriptions aren't transferable.

Q: What about Epic Games?
A: Epic's terms say your licence is personal and non-transferable, and you can't sell, give away or trade your Epic Games Account.

Q: What about PlayStation?
A: PlayStation's Australian terms say your licence to use Digital Products is not transferable unless local law says it must be.

Q: What about Xbox?
A: The Microsoft Services Agreement gives you a personal, non-transferable licence to Xbox game currency and virtual goods. Microsoft accounts are closed automatically after two years of inactivity if no one can sign in.

Q: What about GOG?
A: We couldn't verify a published GOG bereavement policy from an official source. Contact GOG Support with a death certificate.


## Best digital legacy vaults (2026)
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/best/best-digital-legacy-vaults/

For most people, the best digital legacy setup is a password manager with emergency access (Bitwarden or Keeper) plus a planning vault for documents and wishes (Everplans, Prisidio or GoodTrust). The free Google and Apple legacy settings belong on top of either.

Key facts:
- #1 Everplans: Organised planners who want a guided inventory of accounts, wishes and documents.
- #2 Prisidio: US households who want one shared vault for documents, valuables and stories.
- #3 GoodTrust: US families who want estate documents and digital-account planning in one place.
- #4 Bitwarden: Budget-conscious people who want a proper, tested emergency-access workflow.
- #5 Keeper: People who want emergency access alongside business-grade security features.
- #6 Trustworthy: Families who want one organised, shareable place for important documents.
- #7 MyWishes: People who want a free way to record digital and end-of-life wishes.
- #8 SecureSafe: Existing SecureSafe Classic users who already set up data inheritance.
- #9 Life Ledger: Families handling a UK estate who want to notify many companies at once.
- #10 Settld: Families handling a UK estate after a death.

Q: What are the best digital legacy vaults?
A: For most people, the best digital legacy setup is a password manager with emergency access (Bitwarden or Keeper) plus a planning vault for documents and wishes (Everplans, Prisidio or GoodTrust). The free Google and Apple legacy settings belong on top of either.

Q: Is Everplans a good choice?
A: A well-structured digital vault for life admin and end-of-life plans that you can securely share with people you trust.

Q: Is Prisidio a good choice?
A: A family 'life readiness' vault with a Co-Owner and a Keyholder who can get the vault after a verified death, with identity checks via CLEAR.

Q: Is GoodTrust a good choice?
A: An all-in-one US estate planning platform: will, trust and directives (valid in all 50 states) plus a Digital Vault for your digital life.

Q: Is Bitwarden a good choice?
A: The best-value password manager with real emergency access: trusted contacts can request View or Takeover access after a wait time you set.


## Best crypto inheritance tools (2026)
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/best/best-crypto-inheritance-tools/

Casa and Unchained are the strongest choices for Bitcoin inheritance using multisig. Vault12 Guard suits people with many wallets who want social-recovery seed backup. Ledger Recover is a recovery service first and an inheritance tool second.

Key facts:
- #1 Casa: Bitcoin holders who want self-custody plus a guided inheritance plan.
- #2 Unchained: Larger Bitcoin holdings, especially in the US, where a formal inheritance process is worth paying for.
- #3 Vault12 Guard: Self-custody users with many wallets who don't want a seed phrase stored in one place.
- #4 Ledger Recover: Ledger owners worried about losing their seed phrase who accept ID verification.
- #5 Bitkey: Bitcoin holders who want simple self-custody with inheritance built in.
- #6 Nunchuk: Bitcoin holders who want timelock-based inheritance without KYC.
- #7 Liana: Technical bitcoin holders who want DIY inheritance with no company holding keys.
- #8 AnchorWatch: Larger bitcoin holders who want insured, documented inheritance.

Q: What are the best crypto inheritance tools?
A: Casa and Unchained are the strongest choices for Bitcoin inheritance using multisig. Vault12 Guard suits people with many wallets who want social-recovery seed backup. Ledger Recover is a recovery service first and an inheritance tool second.

Q: Is Casa a good choice?
A: A leading multisig self-custody service with inheritance included in every plan, covering bitcoin, ETH and stablecoins.

Q: Is Unchained a good choice?
A: Collaborative-custody Bitcoin vaults (2-of-3 multisig) with inheritance planning. Strong for larger holdings.

Q: Is Vault12 Guard a good choice?
A: Backs up seed phrases using trusted 'Guardians' and lets you name a beneficiary who can inherit after a 48-hour owner veto window and Guardian approvals.

Q: Is Ledger Recover a good choice?
A: An optional, ID-based seed backup for Ledger hardware wallets. Handy for recovery, but it's a trust trade-off and isn't primarily an inheritance tool.


## Best password managers for emergency access (2026)
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/best/best-password-managers-emergency-access/

Bitwarden is the best password manager for emergency access: affordable, open source and with View or Takeover access. Keeper is a strong alternative. 1Password relies on its Emergency Kit and family recovery. Dashlane no longer has an emergency contact feature.

Key facts:
- #1 Bitwarden: Budget-conscious people who want a proper, tested emergency-access workflow.
- #2 Keeper: People who want emergency access alongside business-grade security features.
- #3 Proton Pass (Proton Emergency Access): Proton users who want one emergency process covering Proton Mail, Pass and Drive.
- #4 LastPass Emergency Access: Existing LastPass users who want to add emergency contacts without switching.
- #5 1Password: Families who will store the Emergency Kit with their will and use a Families plan, where an organiser can help recover members' accounts.
- #6 Dashlane: People who use Dashlane for day-to-day passwords and plan legacy access some other way.

Q: What are the best password managers for emergency access?
A: Bitwarden is the best password manager for emergency access: affordable, open source and with View or Takeover access. Keeper is a strong alternative. 1Password relies on its Emergency Kit and family recovery. Dashlane no longer has an emergency contact feature.

Q: Is Bitwarden a good choice?
A: The best-value password manager with real emergency access: trusted contacts can request View or Takeover access after a wait time you set.

Q: Is Keeper a good choice?
A: A solid choice with built-in Emergency Access: name trusted contacts who can request your vault after a wait period.

Q: Is Proton Pass (Proton Emergency Access) a good choice?
A: A solid privacy-first option: on any paid Proton plan you can name up to five emergency contacts who get access automatically after a wait time you choose, unless you deny the request.

Q: Is LastPass Emergency Access a good choice?
A: It works: contacts can request vault access after a wait period. LastPass's 2022 security breaches are a good reason to look at alternatives first, though.


## How to export your Google data with Google Takeout
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/guides/google-takeout-export/

Google Takeout (takeout.google.com) lets you download a copy of your Gmail, Google Photos, Drive and other Google data as .zip or .tgz archives, either once or on a recurring schedule. It's free and works in any browser.

Key facts:
- 8 steps
- Free to do
- Based on official platform and government pages

Steps:
1. Go to takeout.google.com and sign in.
2. Leave everything ticked, or 'Deselect all' and pick products such as Google Photos, Mail and Drive.
3. Click 'Next step' and choose a destination: download link by email, or add to Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive or Box.
4. Choose 'Export once' or 'Export every 2 months for 1 year'.
5. Choose file type (.zip or .tgz) and maximum archive size (larger sizes mean fewer files).
6. Click 'Create export'. Large libraries can take hours or days; Google emails you when it's ready.
7. Download the archives before the links expire and store them on an external drive plus a second location.
8. Record where the backup lives in your digital estate checklist.

Q: Does Google Takeout include Google Photos?
A: Yes. Select Google Photos; photos come with JSON metadata files alongside them.

Q: Is Google Takeout free?
A: Yes.

Q: What formats does Google Takeout use?
A: You can choose .zip or .tgz archives and a maximum archive size.

Q: Where should I store a Takeout backup?
A: On an external drive plus a second location, and note it in your digital estate checklist.

Q: Why back up if I use Inactive Account Manager?
A: Google can delete personal accounts that are inactive for 2 years, and family requests without a plan aren't guaranteed. An offline copy removes that risk.


## How to set up Apple Legacy Contact (step by step)
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/guides/apple-legacy-contact-setup/

An Apple Legacy Contact is someone you choose who can get your iCloud data after you die, using an access key and your death certificate. It's free, takes about 3 minutes on iPhone, and you can add more than one person. They don't need an Apple device.

Key facts:
- 7 steps
- Free to do
- Based on official platform and government pages

Steps:
1. Make sure your device is up to date and you're signed in with your Apple Account (two-factor authentication on).
2. Open Settings → [your name] → Sign-In & Security → Legacy Contact.
3. Tap 'Add Legacy Contact' and pick someone from Contacts.
4. Choose how to share the access key: send it via Messages (if they use a compatible Apple device) or print a copy.
5. Store a printed copy of the key with your will or estate documents.
6. Tell your Legacy Contact what to do: visit digital-legacy.apple.com with the key and a death certificate.
7. Remember that Keychain passwords aren't included, so also set up emergency access in your password manager.

Q: How many Legacy Contacts can I have?
A: You can add more than one. Apple's page doesn't state a fixed limit.

Q: Do Legacy Contacts need an iPhone?
A: No. They can use the printed access key at digital-legacy.apple.com.

Q: What data can't a Legacy Contact get?
A: iCloud Keychain (passwords, passkeys, payment info) and purchased movies, music, books and subscriptions.

Q: What will my Legacy Contact need?
A: The access key you generate and your death certificate. Requirements vary by country; Japan, for example, uses a family certificate.

Q: What devices do I need to set it up?
A: An Apple device running iOS 15.2, iPadOS 15.2 or macOS Monterey 12.1 or later, with two-factor authentication on.


## The complete digital estate checklist
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/guides/digital-estate-checklist/

A digital estate plan has four parts: an inventory of your accounts and assets, a secure way for one trusted person to get access (password manager emergency access), the built-in legacy settings on each platform, and written wishes for each account. This checklist covers all four in about an afternoon.

Key facts:
- 13 steps
- Free to do
- Based on official platform and government pages

Steps:
1. Inventory: list email, social, cloud storage, banks, super/pension, crypto, subscriptions, domains and devices.
2. Password manager: move everything into Bitwarden or Keeper and set up an emergency contact.
3. Google: set up Inactive Account Manager.
4. Apple: add a Legacy Contact and print the key.
5. Facebook: choose a legacy contact or deletion.
6. Microsoft: store your password in your password manager; Microsoft releases content only with a court order.
7. Crypto: document every exchange and wallet; set up an inheritance method for seed phrases (never put seed phrases in your will).
8. Photos: run a Google Takeout or iCloud export and keep an offline copy.
9. Devices: record phone and computer passcodes in your vault, not on paper with your will.
10. Subscriptions: note recurring payments to cancel.
11. Wishes: write what should happen to each account (memorialise, delete, download).
12. Legal: name a digital executor in your will. Laws vary by country and state, so ask a local estate lawyer.
13. Review every 12 months or after big life changes.

Q: What is a digital executor?
A: Someone you nominate to deal with your online accounts. Whether this has legal force depends on where you live.

Q: Should I put passwords in my will?
A: No. Wills can become public documents. Use a password manager with emergency access instead.

Q: Where should I start?
A: Set up emergency access in a password manager, then turn on Google Inactive Account Manager and Apple Legacy Contact. Those three cover most people's essentials.

Q: Is there an Australian version?
A: Yes. See our Australian digital estate guide on wills, executors, probate and the ATO checklist.

Q: How often should I update my plan?
A: Afterkeep suggests reviewing it at least yearly and whenever you open an important account or change devices.


## Digital estate planning in Australia: wills, executors and online accounts
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/guides/australian-digital-estate-guide/

In Australia, your executor manages your estate, including digital assets, after you die. Many banks and platforms want a grant of probate or letters of administration from your state's Supreme Court before releasing money or data. Estates typically take 6 to 12 months. Leave an inventory, not passwords, with your will.

Key facts:
- Probate or letters of administration, if asset holders require them, is usually applied for within 6 months of death in NSW.
- Estate administration typically takes 6 to 12 months (ATO).

Steps:
1. Make or update a valid will and name an executor; NSW's guide notes this can be family, a friend, a solicitor or NSW Trustee and Guardian.
2. List your digital assets: email, cloud storage, socials, PayPal, crypto exchanges, wallets, domains and subscriptions.
3. Store logins in a password manager with emergency access rather than in the will.
4. Switch on the free platform tools: Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, a Facebook legacy contact.
5. After a death: get the death certificate, find the will, and notify organisations. The Australian Death Notification Service can notify several at once.
6. Phone the ATO to pause tax correspondence and decide who will manage the deceased's affairs.
7. Ask each asset holder whether they need a grant; small or jointly held assets may not.
8. Apply to the Supreme Court in your state for probate (with a will) or letters of administration (without one) if needed.
9. Collect assets, pay debts and tax, then distribute. In NSW, executors usually shouldn't distribute earlier than 6 months after death.

Q: Do I need probate for digital accounts in Australia?
A: It depends on the asset holder. The Supreme Court of Victoria says to ask each holder whether it needs a grant; PayPal Australia, for example, asks for a grant of probate or letters of administration.

Q: How long does an estate take in Australia?
A: The ATO says administration typically takes 6 to 12 months but can take longer.

Q: Does Apple need a court order in Australia?
A: Apple says Australia is one of the jurisdictions where it accepts alternative documentation instead of a court order.

Q: Should I put passwords in my Australian will?
A: No. A will can be read by others after death. Keep passwords in a password manager with emergency access and keep an inventory with your will.

Q: What is the difference between probate and letters of administration?
A: Probate is granted to the executor named in a valid will. Letters of administration are issued when there's no valid will, usually to the closest next of kin.

Q: Is probate the same in every Australian state?
A: No. Each state and territory's Supreme Court runs its own probate registry with its own forms, notice rules and fees. See the state-by-state table on this page.


## How to access a deceased person's phone and online accounts
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/guides/access-deceased-persons-phone-and-accounts/

Usually you can't simply log in. Apple can't remove an iPhone passcode without erasing the device, and Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn and others never share passwords. Your real options are a legacy feature they set up, the passcode or a password manager they shared, or a formal request with a death certificate and legal authority.

Key facts:
- Google, Apple, Dropbox and most others publish no fixed processing time.
- Microsoft freezes Outlook.com and OneDrive after 1 year of inactivity.

Steps:
1. Check for a plan first: an Apple Legacy Contact key, a Google Inactive Account Manager email, or emergency access in a password manager.
2. Look for a passcode or password list in their estate papers.
3. Keep phones and computers charged and safe; synced folders (like Dropbox) and local WhatsApp chats may only exist on the device.
4. Get several certified copies of the death certificate.
5. Identify who has legal authority: the executor, or an administrator appointed by the court.
6. Use each platform's official deceased-user process (see the links below). Request data before closure; Google says it can't release contents after closing an account.
7. Expect court orders for content at Microsoft and Dropbox. Apple accepts alternative documents in Australia and some other countries.
8. Cancel subscriptions and payments through the bank if you can't get into the account.

Q: Can Apple unlock a dead person's iPhone?
A: No. Apple says it can't remove a passcode lock without erasing the device, though it may help remove Activation Lock so the device can be reused.

Q: Can I get a deceased parent's emails?
A: Gmail: through Google's deceased-user request, reviewed case by case. Outlook.com: only with a valid subpoena or court order.

Q: Is it legal to log in with their password?
A: Many platform terms prohibit it, and laws vary. Speak to the executor or a lawyer before using someone else's credentials.

Q: What documents do I usually need?
A: A death certificate, your photo ID and, for anything beyond memorialisation, proof of legal authority such as probate or letters of administration.


## What to do when someone dies: the executor's digital checklist (first 30 days)
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/guides/what-to-do-when-someone-dies-digital-checklist/

In the first 30 days, an executor should secure the person's devices, find any legacy plan they left, list their accounts, save irreplaceable photos and files, and then use each platform's official deceased-user process. Request data before closing accounts, and check whether probate is needed. A printable PDF version is below.

Key facts:
- 13 steps over 30 days
- Free printable PDF
- Request data before closing accounts

Steps:
1. Days 1–3: Get several certified copies of the death certificate (or the interim document your state provides).
2. Days 1–3: Secure their phone, laptop and tablets. Keep them charged; don't factory-reset anything yet.
3. Days 1–3: Look for a plan: password manager emergency access, an Apple Legacy Contact access key, a Google Inactive Account Manager email, and a list of accounts.
4. Days 1–7: Find the will and confirm who the executor is. If there's no will, find out who can apply to be administrator.
5. Days 1–7: Don't log in with their password unless a lawyer says it's OK; many platform terms forbid it.
6. Week 1: List every account you can find: email, cloud storage, socials, banks, PayPal, crypto, domains and subscriptions.
7. Week 1: Download or preserve irreplaceable photos and files first, through official legacy tools or deceased-user requests.
8. Week 2: Use each platform's official deceased-user process. Request data before asking for closure.
9. Week 2: In Australia, use the free Australian Death Notification Service to notify participating organisations.
10. Weeks 2–4: Cancel or pause paid subscriptions to stop charges.
11. Weeks 2–4: Memorialise or close social media accounts (Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X) according to the family's wishes.
12. Weeks 2–4: Check whether asset holders need probate or letters of administration, and start the application with your state's Supreme Court if they do.
13. Day 30: Record what's done, what's pending and every reference number. Keep copies of everything you sent.

Q: What should an executor do first with digital accounts?
A: Secure the devices, get certified death certificates, and look for a legacy plan such as password manager emergency access or an Apple Legacy Contact key. Don't reset devices or close accounts yet.

Q: Should I close accounts straight away?
A: No. Request data first. Closing an account can stop you getting its content later.

Q: Can I log in with their password?
A: Many platform terms prohibit it and laws vary. Ask the executor's lawyer before using someone else's credentials.

Q: Do I need probate for online accounts?
A: It depends on the asset holder. Many banks and platforms ask for a grant of probate or letters of administration before releasing money or data.

Q: Is there a printable version?
A: Yes. Download the free PDF checklist from this page.


## Bitwarden vs 1Password for emergency access
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/compare/bitwarden-vs-1password-emergency-access/

For emergency access, Bitwarden wins. Its built-in Emergency Access lets trusted contacts request View or Takeover access, granted when you approve or after a wait time you set. 1Password has no equivalent; you rely on a printed Emergency Kit and, on family plans, an organiser who can recover a member's account.

Key facts:
- Verdict: Choose Bitwarden if you want a tested, automatic emergency-access process.
- Bitwarden: Free plan available; Emergency Access requires Premium or a paid Families/Teams/Enterprise plan. Check current pricing.
- 1Password: Paid plans only (free trial). Check current pricing.

Verdict: Choose Bitwarden if you want a tested, automatic emergency-access process. Choose 1Password only if you'll store the Emergency Kit safely (with your account password written in) and use a Families plan with two organisers.
- Built-in emergency access: Bitwarden: Yes: trusted contacts request access | 1Password: No
- How a trusted person gets in: Bitwarden: Request approved by you, or automatically after your wait time | 1Password: Using your Emergency Kit (sign-in address, email, Secret Key, password)
- Access levels: Bitwarden: View or Takeover (new master password) | 1Password: Full account access via the Kit
- Who can be a contact: Bitwarden: Any free or premium Bitwarden user on the same server | 1Password: Anyone you give the Kit to
- Number of contacts: Bitwarden: No limit | 1Password: N/A
- Plan needed: Bitwarden: Premium or a paid Families/Teams/Enterprise plan | 1Password: Any account; family recovery needs a Families or business plan
- Family recovery: Bitwarden: Organisation account recovery (admins) | 1Password: Family organisers can recover members' accounts

Q: Bitwarden vs 1Password for emergency access: which is better?
A: For emergency access, Bitwarden wins. Its built-in Emergency Access lets trusted contacts request View or Takeover access, granted when you approve or after a wait time you set. 1Password has no equivalent; you rely on a printed Emergency Kit and, on family plans, an organiser who can recover a member's account.

Q: Does 1Password have emergency access?
A: Not as an automatic feature. 1Password's Emergency Kit is a PDF with your sign-in details and a space for your password, which you can give to someone you trust. Family organisers can also recover family members' accounts.

Q: How does Bitwarden emergency access work?
A: You invite a trusted contact and choose View or Takeover access. When they request access, you can approve or reject it; otherwise access is granted after the wait time you set.

Q: Is Bitwarden emergency access free?
A: Adding trusted contacts needs Premium or a paid organisation plan, but the contact only needs a free Bitwarden account on the same server.

Q: Can a 1Password family organiser get into my vault after I die?
A: An organiser can begin recovery, but you must confirm by email and create a new password, so on its own it's not a death-planning tool. Pair it with a stored Emergency Kit.


## GoodTrust vs Everplans
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/compare/goodtrust-vs-everplans/

GoodTrust is the better pick if you need US legal documents: its US$149 Estate+ plan includes a will, trust and directives valid in all 50 US states, plus a Digital Vault. Everplans is a better organiser and sharing vault, free for up to 3 items or US$99.99 a year for Premium, but it doesn't create legal documents.

Key facts:
- Verdict: Pick GoodTrust to make a US will or trust and record digital assets in one place.
- GoodTrust: Estate+ plan advertised at $149 (US). Check current pricing.
- Everplans: Free base app; Everplans Premium is paid. Check current pricing.

Verdict: Pick GoodTrust to make a US will or trust and record digital assets in one place. Pick Everplans to organise documents, accounts and wishes and share them with family. Australians should get legal documents locally either way.
- Main purpose: GoodTrust: US estate planning documents plus a Digital Vault | Everplans: Organising and securely sharing documents, accounts and wishes
- Creates a will or trust: GoodTrust: Yes, will, trust and directives valid in all 50 US states | Everplans: No
- Digital assets vault: GoodTrust: Smart Digital Vault | Everplans: Yes (accounts, documents, wishes)
- Sharing with family: GoodTrust: You choose who gets access and when | Everplans: Secure sharing (Premium)
- Free option: GoodTrust: Not listed on the pricing page | Everplans: Free: up to 3 items
- Paid price (USD): GoodTrust: US$149 Estate+ (one price, one year of unlimited updates) | Everplans: US$99.99/year Premium
- Family members: GoodTrust: Each adult can create their own plan at no extra cost | Everplans: Per account

Q: GoodTrust vs Everplans: which is better?
A: GoodTrust is the better pick if you need US legal documents: its US$149 Estate+ plan includes a will, trust and directives valid in all 50 US states, plus a Digital Vault. Everplans is a better organiser and sharing vault, free for up to 3 items or US$99.99 a year for Premium, but it doesn't create legal documents.

Q: Is GoodTrust or Everplans better for wills?
A: GoodTrust. It creates US wills and trusts; Everplans doesn't create legal documents.

Q: How much do GoodTrust and Everplans cost?
A: GoodTrust's Estate+ plan is listed at US$149. Everplans is free for up to 3 items, and Premium is US$99.99 a year. Prices are from each company's pricing page and may change.

Q: Do they work in Australia?
A: GoodTrust's documents are for the 50 US states. Everplans can organise information anywhere, but its guidance is US-oriented. Australians should make their will under local law.

Q: Do I still need a password manager?
A: Yes. Neither replaces a password manager with emergency access for day-to-day logins.


## Google Inactive Account Manager vs Apple Legacy Contact
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/compare/google-inactive-account-manager-vs-apple-legacy-contact/

They solve the same problem for different ecosystems, and both are free, so use both if you have Google and Apple accounts. Google's Inactive Account Manager acts automatically after a period of inactivity and can share data with up to 10 people. Apple Legacy Contact needs an access key plus a death certificate.

Key facts:
- Verdict: Not either-or: set up both.
- Google Inactive Account Manager: Free.
- Apple Legacy Contact: Free (requires an Apple Account and a supported OS version).

Verdict: Not either-or: set up both. Google's is automatic and flexible but triggers on inactivity, not death. Apple's is triggered by verified death and gives broader account data, but excludes Keychain passwords and purchased media.
- Cost: Google Inactive Account Manager: Free | Apple Legacy Contact: Free
- Trigger: Google Inactive Account Manager: Account inactive for a period you choose | Apple Legacy Contact: Contact submits access key + death certificate
- Number of people: Google Inactive Account Manager: Up to 10 | Apple Legacy Contact: One or more
- What they get: Google Inactive Account Manager: The data types you choose (e.g. Mail, Drive, YouTube) via download link | Apple Legacy Contact: Photos, messages, notes, files, device backups and more
- Excluded: Google Inactive Account Manager: Some information can't be shared | Apple Legacy Contact: iCloud Keychain (passwords, passkeys, payment info), purchased media
- Can delete account: Google Inactive Account Manager: Yes, optional | Apple Legacy Contact: Contact can choose to delete
- Setup: Google Inactive Account Manager: Inactive Account Manager page in your Google Account | Apple Legacy Contact: Settings → [name] → Sign-In & Security → Legacy Contact

Q: Google Inactive Account Manager vs Apple Legacy Contact: which is better?
A: They solve the same problem for different ecosystems, and both are free, so use both if you have Google and Apple accounts. Google's Inactive Account Manager acts automatically after a period of inactivity and can share data with up to 10 people. Apple Legacy Contact needs an access key plus a death certificate.

Q: How long does each one wait or last?
A: Google's Inactive Account Manager acts after an inactivity period you choose, between 3 and 18 months. Apple Legacy Contact access lasts 3 years from the first approved request, then the legacy account is deleted.

Q: Does Apple Legacy Contact remove Activation Lock?
A: Yes. Once access is approved, Apple removes Activation Lock from devices using the original Apple Account.

Q: Should I use both?
A: Yes, if you use Google and Apple services. They cover different accounts and both are free.

Q: Does Google need a death certificate?
A: Not for Inactive Account Manager. It triggers after the inactivity period you set. Without a plan, Google's deceased-user requests do require documentation.

Q: Does either share passwords?
A: Neither shares your password. Apple excludes iCloud Keychain, and Google never provides login details.

Q: What happens if I don't set them up?
A: Google can delete personal accounts inactive for 2 years, and Apple generally needs a court order or local equivalent.


## Bitwarden vs 1Password vs Keeper for emergency access
URL: https://afterkeep.github.io/compare/bitwarden-vs-1password-vs-keeper-emergency-access/

Bitwarden and Keeper both have built-in emergency access; 1Password doesn't. Bitwarden lets trusted contacts request View or Takeover access after a wait time you set, with Premium listed at US$19.80 a year (checked 15 Oct 2026). Keeper allows up to 5 contacts with an optional delay of up to 3 months. 1Password relies on a printed Emergency Kit.

Q: Which has the best emergency access: Bitwarden, 1Password or Keeper?
A: Bitwarden, for most people: built-in requests, View or Takeover access, and a wait time you control. Keeper is a strong alternative. 1Password has no built-in emergency access.

Q: How much does Bitwarden Premium cost?
A: Bitwarden's pricing page lists Premium at US$19.80 a year (checked 15 Oct 2026).

Q: How many emergency contacts can I have?
A: Bitwarden: no limit stated. Keeper: up to 5. 1Password: anyone you give your Emergency Kit to.

A: No. Afterkeep is a comparison and guide directory only.
